extracted.intended_audience: physicians, apothecaries, natural philosophers, early chemists/alchemists
extracted.subtask_description: Practical/tests-oriented natural-philosophical guidance for recognising properties of mixtures (wine, water, oil, honey), detecting adulteration, and identifying metals, bitumens, and amber in soils and materials by sensory, physical and simple experimental tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tests for whether wine and water truly mix
rubrics_metrics.description: Wine and water often do not form a perfect homogeneous mixture; apparent mixing can be tested by absorption and layering experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical tests: put a linen (linteum) into the wine-water mixture — water will be drawn out and appear on the linen while the wine's form remains; pour wine on a bread crust and then pour the water — observe whether wine remains separated/‘supernates’. If water can be drawn off leaving wine-like residue, the liquids are not perfectly mixed. Use such observations to conclude that a true mixture would not allow such separations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Layering/floatation to determine relative specific gravity
rubrics_metrics.description: Liquids arrange by weight: the lighter floats above the heavier; e.g., oil floats on wine and wine on water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe which liquid floats when two are placed together: olive oil will float above wine; wine will float above water. Use this to infer relative lightness/heaviness of liquids and to decide which substance is 'supernatant'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detecting adulteration in wine by sedimentation, turbidity, color and taste
rubrics_metrics.description: Adulterants and heavy powders in wine settle to the bottom, change clarity, color and taste; metals and certain substances leave diagnostic residues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leave wine in a glass or vessel for hours: metallic adulterants tend to sink and form a metallic residue at the bottom; altered color or persistent turbidity indicates corruption. Smell and taste (metallic taste, unpleasant odors) help detect fraud. Heating or adding reagents (e.g., a few metallic drops) can precipitate adulterants and reveal honey or metallic additions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detecting honey (mellis) adulteration in wine
rubrics_metrics.description: Honey mixed in wine alters its behaviour and can be recognised by reactions with metals and by differences in suspension/settling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If honey is present in wine, certain simple additions or observations show it: metal additions or certain clarifying steps make the honey-associated substance remain or behave differently than pure wine (the text notes that wine made with honey shows resolute residues when tested with metal). Observe viscosity, tendency to remain suspended, and response to clarifying agents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oil adulteration and behaviour in mixtures
rubrics_metrics.description: Adulterated oil displays distinctive burning, sediment and mixing properties and interacts with water and wine in predictable ways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tests: burn a sample — adulterated oil may crackle or sputter, produce greater amurca (sediment), or collect more impurities; mix oil with wine or water and heat — oil will resist mixing and ascend by heat/transpiration; fine grinding or adding wax improves thin oils. Use these observations to judge oil quality and adulteration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of heat and sweating for separation of oil and water
rubrics_metrics.description: When oil and water are combined and heated in a vessel, water tends to be exhausted first and oil resists exhaustion; cooling and sweating affect receptivity to heat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: when oil and water are layered and heated, water will be driven off before oil; oil yields by sweating through pores and by heat. Observe which liquid evaporates or persists to determine true mixture versus mere juxtaposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of metals in mountains and soils by colour, odour and halitus
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain colours of earth/rocks and an acrid sulphurous halitus indicate the presence and kind of metals in a location.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey mountains and rocks: greenish, black, purple, livid, ashy hues associate with silver/gold/pyrite/lead/sulphur respectively. A sulphurous smell rising from fissures is a sign of metalliferous ground. Also examine surfaces for metallic glints and fractured veins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vegetation as an indicator of metalliferous ground
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific plants or plant characteristics frequently accompany metal-rich soils and can be used as indicators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe local flora: plants that are pallid, deciduous, small-fruited or spiny (juniper low, ivy, caprifig, many thorny species) often grow where metals abound; such plants may be stunted or have thin leaves. Conversely, fertile and fruit-bearing vegetation usually signals non-metallic soils.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testing for metal by liquefaction and melting
rubrics_metrics.description: Subjecting suspect stone or earth to heat and observing liquefaction, metallic sheen, or separation of metal identifies metallic content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heat a portion of the material: if a shining metallic portion appears on melting or a metallic bead forms, the presence and possibly the quantity of metal are indicated. Some metals will show metallic particles descending in liquids on cooling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Density/weight and sedimentation as indicators of metallic matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Heaviness or descent of particulate matter in liquids betrays the presence of denser metallic substances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe whether portions of material sink in a vessel or in wine; heavy (grave) parts will descend and collect at the bottom. Repeated settling of heavy particles over time may show a vestige of metal in the deposit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing different lapides (stones) and metallic matter by texture, veins and fracture
rubrics_metrics.description: Metallic stones and ores show particular textures: veins, firmness, colour, and inner veins or 'venae' within the substance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inspect fractured surfaces: the presence of veins, harder or more compact portions, and internal structure differing from ordinary earth indicate a metallic nature. Some are firmer and colder; others are softened by abundant fatness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification and uses of alum (alumen)
rubrics_metrics.description: Alum is astringent and useful to clarify and preserve materials and liquids; it has characteristic effects on fabrics, leather and on wine when present in vessels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical signs: alum makes feathers of geese better, improves leather, and prevents wine from clouding in vessels. Preparation: boil alum-containing waters until one third remains; the residue is a sign of alum. Alum also manifests by astringent taste and certain stinging properties on contact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification and recognition of bitumens, asphalt, petroleum and related substances
rubrics_metrics.description: Bitumens vary by colour, smell and medicinal/combustion properties; some are fragrant and purifying when burnt, others foul and injurious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish kinds by smell (sweet/pleasant vs acrid), colour (white, black, etc.), and burning behaviour (some burn clean with fragrant smoke useful for fumigation, others foul). Note origins (sea or terrestrial) and local cures: some bitumens prevent pestilence when burned, and some spots show vegetation failure near heavy petroleum seeps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of amber (succinum) and its varieties
rubrics_metrics.description: Amber (succinum) is distinguished by translucence, inclusion of small organisms, specific smells on burning, attraction properties when heated, and types ranging from white fragrant to black heavy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicators: amber often contains insects, plant fragments, and remains translucent; heated/rubbed it attracts palea/straw and small light things; when burnt it yields a pleasant odor (similar to myrrh); different kinds (white fragrant, black odorless) have different weights and smells. Amber preserves organic inclusions and resists putrefaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing amber (succinum) from magnetite by attraction tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Amber and magnet have different attractive behaviours: amber attracts light vegetable matter when heated or rubbed, while magnet attracts iron.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test attraction: heat or rub succinum and observe attraction of straw, chaff or small plant fragments; it will not move iron. A magnet will attract iron but not straw or the same behaviour as amber. Use friction/heat to enhance amber's attraction.
